    23→## 1. Overview and Goals
    24→
    25→### 1.1 Problem Statement
    26→
    27→A coding agent is a system that takes a natural language instruction ("fix the login bug", "add dark mode", "write tests for this module"), plans a solution, and executes it by reading files, editing code, running commands, and iterating until the task is done. The core challenge is orchestrating an agentic loop that coordinates LLM calls, tool execution, context management, and provider-specific behavior into a reliable autonomous workflow.
    28→
    29→Each LLM provider's models are trained and optimized for specific tool interfaces and system prompts. GPT-5.2 and the GPT-5.2-codex series work best with the same tools and prompts as codex-rs. Gemini models work best with the same tools and prompts as gemini-cli. Anthropic models work best with the same tools and prompts as Claude Code. A good coding agent respects this reality rather than forcing a universal toolset on all models.
    30→
    31→### 1.2 Why a Library, Not a CLI
    32→
    33→Tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI exist as end-user CLIs. You can run them in non-interactive mode and pipe output, but that gives you a black box: text goes in, text comes out. You cannot programmatically inspect the conversation mid-run, inject steering messages between tool calls, swap the execution environment, change reasoning effort on the fly, observe individual tool calls as they happen, or compose agents into larger systems.
    34→
    35→This spec defines a **library** -- a programmable agentic loop that a host application controls at every step. The host can:
    36→
    37→- **Submit input and observe every event** as the agent thinks, calls tools, and produces output -- not after the fact, but in real time as it happens.
    38→- **Steer the agent mid-task** by injecting messages between tool rounds, redirecting it without restarting.
    39→- **Change configuration on the fly** -- reasoning effort, model, timeouts -- between any two turns.
    40→- **Swap where tools run** by providing a different execution environment (local, Docker, Kubernetes, WASM, SSH) without changing any tool logic.
    41→- **Compose agents** by spawning subagents for parallel work, each with their own history but sharing the same filesystem.
    42→- **Build on top of it** -- CLIs, IDEs, web UIs, batch systems, CI pipelines, evaluation harnesses, and agent-to-agent coordination systems all consume the same library.
    43→
    44→The fidelity of control is the point. Every coding agent CLI is built on an agentic loop internally; this spec makes that loop a first-class, programmable interface.
    45→
    46→### 1.3 Design Principles
    47→
    48→**Programmable-first.** The agent is a library, not a CLI. Every aspect of the loop -- tool execution, event delivery, steering, configuration -- is accessible programmatically. A CLI is one possible host application, not the primary interface.
    49→
    50→**Provider-aligned.** Each model family works best with its native agent's tools and system prompts. The spec defines provider-specific tool profiles, not a single universal set. Start from the provider's native toolset and extend it.
    51→
    52→**Extensible execution.** Tool execution is abstracted behind an `ExecutionEnvironment` interface. The default runs locally. Implementations can target Docker, Kubernetes, WASM, or any remote host. Changing where tools run should not require changing the tools themselves.
    53→
    54→**Event-driven.** Every agent action emits a typed event for UI rendering, logging, and integration. The event stream is the primary interface for host applications.
    55→
    56→**Hackable.** Reasonable defaults with override points everywhere -- timeouts, output sizes, tool sets, execution environments, system prompts, reasoning effort. The spec prescribes defaults, not ceilings.
    57→
    58→**Language-agnostic.** All code is pseudocode. Data structures use neutral notation. No specific programming language is assumed.
    59→
    60→### 1.3 Architecture
    61→
    62→```
    63→+--------------------------------------------------+
    64→|  Host Application (CLI, IDE, Web UI)              |
    65→+--------------------------------------------------+
    66→        |                            ^
    67→        | submit(input)              | events
    68→        v                            |
    69→+--------------------------------------------------+
    70→|  Coding Agent Loop                                |
    71→|  +--------------------+  +---------------------+ |
    72→|  | Session            |  | Provider Profiles   | |
    73→|  |  - history         |  |  - OpenAI (codex)   | |
    74→|  |  - steering queue  |  |  - Anthropic (cc)   | |
    75→|  |  - event emitter   |  |  - Gemini (cli)     | |
    76→|  +--------------------+  +---------------------+ |
    77→|  +--------------------+  +---------------------+ |
    78→|  | Tool Registry      |  | Execution Env       | |
    79→|  |  - tool dispatch   |  |  - local (default)  | |
    80→|  |  - truncation      |  |  - docker           | |
    81→|  |  - validation      |  |  - k8s / wasm / ssh | |
    82→|  +--------------------+  +---------------------+ |
    83→+--------------------------------------------------+
    84→        |
    85→        v
    86→+--------------------------------------------------+
    87→|  Unified LLM SDK (Client.complete / stream)       |
    88→+--------------------------------------------------+
    89→        |
    90→        v
    91→+--------------------------------------------------+
    92→|  LLM Provider APIs                                |
    93→|  (OpenAI Responses / Anthropic Messages / Gemini) |
    94→+--------------------------------------------------+
    95→```
    96→
    97→The agent loop does NOT use the Unified LLM SDK's `generate()` high-level function (which has its own tool loop). It uses the low-level `Client.complete()` and implements its own loop because it needs to interleave tool execution with output truncation, steering message injection, event emission, timeout enforcement, and loop detection -- concerns that the SDK's generic tool loop does not handle.

   109→### 1.5 Relationship to the Unified LLM SDK
   110→
   111→This spec assumes the companion Unified LLM Client Specification is implemented. The agent loop imports and uses these types directly:
   112→
   113→- `Client`, `Request`, `Response` -- for LLM communication
   114→- `Message`, `ContentPart`, `Role` -- for conversation history
   115→- `Tool`, `ToolCall`, `ToolResult` -- for tool definitions and results
   116→- `StreamEvent` -- for streaming responses
   117→- `Usage` -- for token tracking
   118→- `FinishReason` -- for stop condition detection
   119→

   122→---
   123→
   124→## 2. Agentic Loop
   125→
   126→### 2.1 Session
   127→
   128→The Session is the central orchestrator. It holds the conversation state, dispatches tool calls, manages the event stream, and enforces limits.
   129→
   130→```
   131→RECORD Session:
   132→    id                : String                  -- UUID, assigned at creation
   133→    provider_profile  : ProviderProfile         -- tools + system prompt for the active model
   134→    execution_env     : ExecutionEnvironment    -- where tools run
   135→    history           : List<Turn>              -- ordered conversation turns
   136→    event_emitter     : EventEmitter            -- delivers events to host application
   137→    config            : SessionConfig           -- limits, timeouts, settings
   138→    state             : SessionState            -- current lifecycle state
   139→    llm_client        : Client                  -- from the Unified LLM SDK
   140→    steering_queue    : Queue<String>           -- messages to inject between tool rounds
   141→    followup_queue    : Queue<String>           -- messages to process after current input completes
   142→    subagents         : Map<String, SubAgent>   -- active child agents
   143→```
   144→
   145→### 2.2 Session Configuration
   146→
   147→```
   148→RECORD SessionConfig:
   149→    max_turns                   : Integer = 0       -- 0 = unlimited
   150→    max_tool_rounds_per_input   : Integer = 0       -- 0 = unlimited, per user input, not per session
   151→    default_command_timeout_ms  : Integer = 10000   -- 10 seconds
   152→    max_command_timeout_ms      : Integer = 600000  -- 10 minutes
   153→    reasoning_effort            : String | None     -- "low", "medium", "high", or null
   154→    tool_output_limits          : Map<String, Integer>  -- per-tool char limits (see Section 5)
   155→    enable_loop_detection       : Boolean = true
   156→    loop_detection_window       : Integer = 10      -- consecutive identical calls before warning
   157→    max_subagent_depth          : Integer = 1       -- max nesting level for subagents
   158→```
   159→
   160→### 2.3 Session Lifecycle
   161→
   162→```
   163→ENUM SessionState:
   164→    IDLE              -- waiting for user input
   165→    PROCESSING        -- running the agentic loop
   166→    AWAITING_INPUT    -- model asked the user a question
   167→    CLOSED            -- session terminated (normal or error)
   168→```
   169→
   170→State transitions:
   171→
   172→```
   173→IDLE -> PROCESSING          -- on submit()
   174→PROCESSING -> PROCESSING    -- tool loop continues
   175→PROCESSING -> AWAITING_INPUT -- model asks user a question (no tool calls, open-ended)
   176→PROCESSING -> IDLE          -- natural completion or turn limit
   177→PROCESSING -> CLOSED        -- unrecoverable error
   178→IDLE -> CLOSED              -- explicit close()
   179→any -> CLOSED               -- abort signal
   180→AWAITING_INPUT -> PROCESSING -- user provides answer
   181→```
   182→
   183→### 2.4 Turn Types
   184→
   185→A Turn is a single entry in the conversation history.
   186→
   187→```
   188→RECORD UserTurn:
   189→    content     : String
   190→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   191→
   192→RECORD AssistantTurn:
   193→    content     : String            -- text output
   194→    tool_calls  : List<ToolCall>    -- tool invocations requested by the model
   195→    reasoning   : String | None     -- thinking/reasoning text (if available)
   196→    usage       : Usage             -- token counts for this turn
   197→    response_id : String | None     -- provider response ID
   198→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   199→
   200→RECORD ToolResultsTurn:
   201→    results     : List<ToolResult>  -- one per tool call
   202→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   203→
   204→RECORD SystemTurn:
   205→    content     : String
   206→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   207→
   208→RECORD SteeringTurn:
   209→    content     : String            -- injected steering message
   210→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   211→```
   212→
   213→### 2.5 The Core Agentic Loop
   214→
   215→This is the centerpiece of the spec. The loop runs until the model produces a text-only response (no tool calls), a limit is hit, or an abort signal fires.
   216→
   217→```
   218→FUNCTION process_input(session, user_input):
   219→    session.state = PROCESSING
   220→    session.history.APPEND(UserTurn(content = user_input))
   221→    session.emit(USER_INPUT, content = user_input)
   222→
   223→    -- Drain any pending steering messages before the first LLM call
   224→    drain_steering(session)
   225→
   226→    round_count = 0
   227→
   228→    LOOP:
   229→        -- 1. Check limits
   230→        IF session.config.max_tool_rounds_per_input > 0 AND round_count >= session.config.max_tool_rounds_per_input:
   231→            session.emit(TURN_LIMIT, round = round_count)
   232→            BREAK
   233→
   234→        IF session.config.max_turns > 0 AND count_turns(session) >= session.config.max_turns:
   235→            session.emit(TURN_LIMIT, total_turns = count_turns(session))
   236→            BREAK
   237→
   238→        IF session.abort_signaled:
   239→            BREAK
   240→
   241→        -- 2. Build LLM request using provider profile
   242→        system_prompt = session.provider_profile.build_system_prompt(
   243→            environment = session.execution_env,
   244→            project_docs = discover_project_docs(session.execution_env.working_directory())
   245→        )
   246→        messages = convert_history_to_messages(session.history)
   247→        tool_defs = session.provider_profile.tools()
   248→
   249→        request = Request(
   250→            model           = session.provider_profile.model,
   251→            messages        = [Message.system(system_prompt)] + messages,
   252→            tools           = tool_defs,
   253→            tool_choice     = "auto",
   254→            reasoning_effort = session.config.reasoning_effort,
   255→            provider        = session.provider_profile.id,
   256→            provider_options = session.provider_profile.provider_options()
   257→        )
   258→
   259→        -- 3. Call LLM via Unified LLM SDK (single-shot, no SDK-level tool loop)
   260→        response = session.llm_client.complete(request)
   261→
   262→        -- 4. Record assistant turn
   263→        assistant_turn = AssistantTurn(
   264→            content     = response.text,
   265→            tool_calls  = response.tool_calls,
   266→            reasoning   = response.reasoning,
   267→            usage       = response.usage,
   268→            response_id = response.id
   269→        )
   270→        session.history.APPEND(assistant_turn)
   271→        session.emit(ASSISTANT_TEXT_END, text = response.text, reasoning = response.reasoning)
   272→
   273→        -- 5. If no tool calls, natural completion
   274→        IF response.tool_calls IS EMPTY:
   275→            BREAK
   276→
   277→        -- 6. Execute tool calls through the execution environment
   278→        round_count += 1
   279→        results = execute_tool_calls(session, response.tool_calls)
   280→        session.history.APPEND(ToolResultsTurn(results = results))
   281→
   282→        -- 7. Drain steering messages injected during tool execution
   283→        drain_steering(session)
   284→
   285→        -- 8. Loop detection
   286→        IF session.config.enable_loop_detection:
   287→            IF detect_loop(session.history, session.config.loop_detection_window):
   288→                warning = "Loop detected: the last " + session.config.loop_detection_window
   289→                        + " tool calls follow a repeating pattern. Try a different approach."
   290→                session.history.APPEND(SteeringTurn(content = warning))
   291→                session.emit(LOOP_DETECTION, message = warning)
   292→
   293→    END LOOP
   294→
   295→    -- Process follow-up messages if any are queued
   296→    IF session.followup_queue IS NOT EMPTY:
   297→        next_input = session.followup_queue.DEQUEUE()
   298→        process_input(session, next_input)
   299→        RETURN
   300→
   301→    session.state = IDLE
   302→    session.emit(SESSION_END)
   303→
   304→
   305→FUNCTION drain_steering(session):
   306→    WHILE session.steering_queue IS NOT EMPTY:
   307→        msg = session.steering_queue.DEQUEUE()
   308→        session.history.APPEND(SteeringTurn(content = msg))
   309→        session.emit(STEERING_INJECTED, content = msg)
   310→
   311→
   312→FUNCTION execute_tool_calls(session, tool_calls):
   313→    results = []
   314→
   315→    -- Execute tool calls (concurrently if profile supports parallel execution)
   316→    IF session.provider_profile.supports_parallel_tool_calls AND LENGTH(tool_calls) > 1:
   317→        results = AWAIT_ALL([
   318→            execute_single_tool(session, tc) FOR tc IN tool_calls
   319→        ])
   320→    ELSE:
   321→        FOR EACH tc IN tool_calls:
   322→            result = execute_single_tool(session, tc)
   323→            results.APPEND(result)
   324→    RETURN results
   325→
   326→
   327→FUNCTION execute_single_tool(session, tool_call):
   328→    session.emit(TOOL_CALL_START, tool_name = tool_call.name, call_id = tool_call.id)
   329→
   330→    -- Look up tool in registry
   331→    registered = session.provider_profile.tool_registry.get(tool_call.name)
   332→    IF registered IS None:
   333→        error_msg = "Unknown tool: " + tool_call.name
   334→        session.emit(TOOL_CALL_END, call_id = tool_call.id, error = error_msg)
   335→        RETURN ToolResult(tool_call_id = tool_call.id, content = error_msg, is_error = true)
   336→
   337→    -- Execute via execution environment
   338→    TRY:
   339→        raw_output = registered.execute(tool_call.arguments, session.execution_env)
   340→
   341→        -- Truncate output before sending to LLM (character-based first, then line-based)
   342→        truncated_output = truncate_tool_output(raw_output, tool_call.name, session.config)
   343→
   344→        -- Emit full output via event stream (not truncated)
   345→        session.emit(TOOL_CALL_END, call_id = tool_call.id, output = raw_output)
   346→
   347→        RETURN ToolResult(
   348→            tool_call_id = tool_call.id,
   349→            content = truncated_output,
   350→            is_error = false
   351→        )
   352→
   353→    CATCH error:
   354→        error_msg = "Tool error (" + tool_call.name + "): " + str(error)
   355→        session.emit(TOOL_CALL_END, call_id = tool_call.id, error = error_msg)
   356→        RETURN ToolResult(tool_call_id = tool_call.id, content = error_msg, is_error = true)
   357→```
   358→
   359→### 2.6 Steering
   360→
   361→Steering allows the host application to inject messages into the conversation between tool rounds. This is how a user can redirect the agent mid-task without waiting for it to finish.
   362→
   363→```
   364→session.steer(message: String)
   365→    -- Queue a message to be injected after the current tool round completes.
   366→    -- The message becomes a SteeringTurn in the history, converted to a
   367→    -- user message for the LLM on the next call.
   368→    -- If the agent is idle, the message is delivered on the next submit().
   369→
   370→session.follow_up(message: String)
   371→    -- Queue a message to be processed after the current input is fully handled
   372→    -- (model has produced a text-only response). Triggers a new processing cycle.
   373→```
   374→
   375→SteeringTurns are converted to user-role messages when building the LLM request. This means the model sees them as additional user instructions.
   376→
   377→### 2.7 Reasoning Effort
   378→
   379→The `reasoning_effort` config controls how much reasoning/thinking the model does. It maps directly to the Unified LLM SDK's `reasoning_effort` field on the Request.
   380→
   381→| Value    | Effect                                                           |
   382→|----------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
   383→| "low"    | Minimal reasoning. Faster, cheaper. Good for simple tasks.      |
   384→| "medium" | Balanced reasoning. Default for most tasks.                     |
   385→| "high"   | Deep reasoning. Slower, more expensive. Good for complex tasks. |
   386→| null     | Provider default (no override).                                 |
   387→
   388→Changing `reasoning_effort` mid-session takes effect on the next LLM call. For OpenAI reasoning models (GPT-5.2 series), this controls the reasoning token budget. For Anthropic models with extended thinking, this maps to the thinking budget. For Gemini models with thinking, this maps to thinkingConfig.
   389→
   390→### 2.8 Stop Conditions
   391→
   392→The loop exits when any of these conditions is met:
   393→
   394→1. **Natural completion.** The model responds with text only (no tool calls). The model is done.
   395→2. **Round limit.** `max_tool_rounds_per_input` is reached. The agent stops and returns what it has.
   396→3. **Turn limit.** `max_turns` across the entire session is reached.
   397→4. **Abort signal.** The host application signals cancellation. The current LLM stream is closed, running processes are killed, and the session transitions to CLOSED.
   398→5. **Unrecoverable error.** An authentication error, context overflow, or other non-retryable error. The session transitions to CLOSED.
   399→
   400→### 2.9 Event System
   401→
   402→Every agent action emits a typed event. Events are delivered via an async iterator (or language-appropriate equivalent) to the host application.
   403→
   404→```
   405→RECORD SessionEvent:
   406→    kind        : EventKind
   407→    timestamp   : Timestamp
   408→    session_id  : String
   409→    data        : Map<String, Any>
   410→
   411→ENUM EventKind:
   412→    SESSION_START           -- session created
   413→    SESSION_END             -- session closed (includes final state)
   414→    USER_INPUT              -- user submitted input
   415→    ASSISTANT_TEXT_START     -- model began generating text
   416→    ASSISTANT_TEXT_DELTA     -- incremental text token
   417→    ASSISTANT_TEXT_END       -- model finished text (includes full text)
   418→    TOOL_CALL_START         -- tool execution began (includes tool name, call ID)
   419→    TOOL_CALL_OUTPUT_DELTA  -- incremental tool output (for streaming tools)
   420→    TOOL_CALL_END           -- tool execution finished (includes FULL untruncated output)
   421→    STEERING_INJECTED       -- a steering message was added to history
   422→    TURN_LIMIT              -- a turn limit was hit
   423→    LOOP_DETECTION          -- a loop pattern was detected
   424→    ERROR                   -- an error occurred
   425→```
   426→
   427→**Key design decision:** The `TOOL_CALL_END` event carries the FULL untruncated tool output. The LLM receives the truncated version. This means the host application (UI, logs) always has access to complete output even though the model sees an abbreviated version.
   428→
   429→### 2.10 Loop Detection
   430→
   431→Track the signature of each tool call (name + arguments hash). If the last N calls (default: 10) contain a repeating pattern (e.g., the same 2-3 calls cycling), inject a warning as a SteeringTurn telling the model to try a different approach.
   432→
   433→```
   434→FUNCTION detect_loop(history, window_size) -> Boolean:
   435→    recent_calls = extract_tool_call_signatures(history, last = window_size)
   436→    IF LENGTH(recent_calls) < window_size: RETURN false
   437→
   438→    -- Check for repeating patterns of length 1, 2, or 3
   439→    FOR pattern_len IN [1, 2, 3]:
   440→        IF window_size % pattern_len != 0: CONTINUE
   441→        pattern = recent_calls[0..pattern_len]
   442→        all_match = true
   443→        FOR i FROM pattern_len TO window_size STEP pattern_len:
   444→            IF recent_calls[i..i+pattern_len] != pattern:
   445→                all_match = false
   446→                BREAK
   447→        IF all_match: RETURN true
   448→
   449→    RETURN false
   450→```

   453→
   454→## 3. Provider-Aligned Toolsets
   455→
   456→### 3.1 The Provider Alignment Principle
   457→
   458→Models are trained and optimized for specific tool interfaces. OpenAI's models are trained on codex-rs's apply_patch format and tool schemas. Anthropic's models are trained on Claude Code's old_string/new_string editing and tool schemas. Gemini models are trained on gemini-cli's tool set.
   459→
   460→Using a provider's native tool format produces better results than forcing a universal format. **The initial base for each provider should be a 1:1 copy of the provider's reference agent -- the exact same system prompt, the exact same tool definitions, byte for byte.** Not a similar prompt. Not similar tools. The actual prompt and harness that the model was evaluated and optimized against. Then extend it with additional capabilities (like subagents). Do not make all providers conform to a single tool interface.
   461→
   462→### 3.2 ProviderProfile Interface
   463→
   464→```
   465→INTERFACE ProviderProfile:
   466→    id              : String            -- "openai", "anthropic", "gemini"
   467→    model           : String            -- model identifier (e.g., "gpt-5.2-codex")
   468→    tool_registry   : ToolRegistry      -- all tools available to this profile
   469→
   470→    FUNCTION build_system_prompt(environment, project_docs) -> String
   471→    FUNCTION tools() -> List<ToolDefinition>
   472→    FUNCTION provider_options() -> Map | None
   473→
   474→    -- Capability flags
   475→    supports_reasoning           : Boolean
   476→    supports_streaming           : Boolean
   477→    supports_parallel_tool_calls : Boolean
   478→    context_window_size          : Integer
   479→```
   480→
   481→### 3.3 Shared Core Tools
   482→
   483→All profiles include these base tools. The parameter schemas and output formats may vary between profiles (to match the provider's native conventions), but the functionality is the same.
   484→
   485→#### read_file
   486→
   487→Reads a file's contents with line numbers.
   488→
   489→```
   490→TOOL read_file:
   491→    description: "Read a file from the filesystem. Returns line-numbered content."
   492→    parameters:
   493→        file_path   : String (required)     -- absolute path to the file
   494→        offset      : Integer (optional)    -- 1-based line number to start reading from
   495→        limit       : Integer (optional)    -- max lines to read (default: 2000)
   496→    returns: Line-numbered text content in "NNN | content" format
   497→    errors: File not found, permission denied, binary file
   498→```
   499→
   500→Behavior: Read the file, prepend line numbers, respect offset/limit. For image files, return the image data for multimodal models. For very large files without offset/limit, the tool output will be truncated by the truncation layer (Section 5).
   501→
   502→#### write_file
   503→
   504→Writes content to a file, creating it if it does not exist.
   505→
   506→```
   507→TOOL write_file:
   508→    description: "Write content to a file. Creates the file and parent directories if needed."
   509→    parameters:
   510→        file_path   : String (required)     -- absolute path
   511→        content     : String (required)     -- the full file content
   512→    returns: Confirmation message with bytes written
   513→    errors: Permission denied, disk full
   514→```
   515→
   516→#### edit_file
   517→
   518→Searches for an exact string in a file and replaces it. This is the native editing format for Anthropic models.
   519→
   520→```
   521→TOOL edit_file:
   522→    description: "Replace an exact string occurrence in a file."
   523→    parameters:
   524→        file_path   : String (required)
   525→        old_string  : String (required)     -- exact text to find
   526→        new_string  : String (required)     -- replacement text
   527→        replace_all : Boolean (optional)    -- replace all occurrences (default: false)
   528→    returns: Confirmation with number of replacements made
   529→    errors: File not found, old_string not found, old_string not unique (when replace_all=false)
   530→```
   531→
   532→Behavior: Exact string match. If `old_string` is not found exactly, the implementation may attempt fuzzy matching (whitespace normalization, Unicode equivalence) and report the match. If `old_string` matches multiple locations and `replace_all` is false, return an error asking the model to provide more context.
   533→
   534→#### shell
   535→
   536→Executes a command in the system shell.
   537→
   538→```
   539→TOOL shell:
   540→    description: "Execute a shell command. Returns stdout, stderr, and exit code."
   541→    parameters:
   542→        command     : String (required)     -- the command to run
   543→        timeout_ms  : Integer (optional)    -- override default timeout
   544→        description : String (optional)     -- human-readable description of what this does
   545→    returns: Command output (stdout + stderr), exit code, duration
   546→    errors: Timeout, permission denied, command not found
   547→```
   548→
   549→Behavior: Run in a new process group. Enforce timeout (default from SessionConfig, overridable per-call). On timeout: SIGTERM, wait 2 seconds, SIGKILL. Return collected output plus timeout message. Environment variable filtering applied (see Section 4).
   550→
   551→#### grep
   552→
   553→Searches file contents by pattern.
   554→
   555→```
   556→TOOL grep:
   557→    description: "Search file contents using regex patterns."
   558→    parameters:
   559→        pattern         : String (required)     -- regex pattern
   560→        path            : String (optional)     -- directory or file to search (default: working dir)
   561→        glob_filter     : String (optional)     -- file pattern filter (e.g., "*.py")
   562→        case_insensitive: Boolean (optional)    -- default: false
   563→        max_results     : Integer (optional)    -- default: 100
   564→    returns: Matching lines with file paths and line numbers
   565→    errors: Invalid regex, path not found
   566→```
   567→
   568→#### glob
   569→
   570→Finds files by name pattern.
   571→
   572→```
   573→TOOL glob:
   574→    description: "Find files matching a glob pattern."
   575→    parameters:
   576→        pattern     : String (required)     -- glob pattern (e.g., "**/*.ts")
   577→        path        : String (optional)     -- base directory (default: working dir)
   578→    returns: List of matching file paths, sorted by modification time (newest first)
   579→    errors: Invalid pattern, path not found
   580→```
   581→
   582→### 3.4 OpenAI Profile (codex-rs-aligned)
   583→
   584→For GPT-5.2, GPT-5.2-codex, and other OpenAI models. Mirrors the codex-rs toolset.
   585→
   586→**Key difference: `apply_patch` replaces `edit_file` and `write_file` for file modifications.** OpenAI models are specifically trained on this format and produce significantly better edits when using it.
   587→
   588→Additional/modified tools beyond the shared core:
   589→
   590→#### apply_patch (OpenAI-specific)
   591→
   592→```
   593→TOOL apply_patch:
   594→    description: "Apply code changes using the patch format. Supports creating, deleting,
   595→                  and modifying files in a single operation."
   596→    parameters:
   597→        patch       : String (required)     -- the patch content in v4a format
   598→    returns: List of affected file paths and operations performed
   599→    errors: Parse error, file not found (for updates), verification failure
   600→```
   601→
   602→The patch format is defined in full in [Appendix A](#appendix-a-apply_patch-v4a-format-reference).
   603→
   604→**Profile tool list for OpenAI:**
   605→- `read_file` (same as shared core, maps to codex-rs `read_file`)
   606→- `apply_patch` (replaces `edit_file` and `write_file` for modifications)
   607→- `write_file` (kept for creating new files without patch overhead)
   608→- `shell` (maps to codex-rs `exec_command`, 10s default timeout)
   609→- `grep` (maps to codex-rs `grep_files`)
   610→- `glob` (maps to codex-rs `list_dir`)
   611→- `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `wait`, `close_agent` (subagent tools, Section 7)
   612→
   613→**System prompt:** Should mirror the codex-rs system prompt structure. Cover identity, tool usage guidelines, the apply_patch format expectations, and coding best practices.
   614→
   615→**Provider options:** The OpenAI profile should set `reasoning.effort` on the Responses API request when `reasoning_effort` is configured.
   616→
   617→### 3.5 Anthropic Profile (Claude Code-aligned)
   618→
   619→For Claude Opus 4.6, Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, and older Claude models. Mirrors the Claude Code toolset.
   620→
   621→**Key difference: `edit_file` with `old_string`/`new_string` is the native editing format.** Anthropic models are specifically trained on this exact-match search-and-replace pattern. Do NOT use apply_patch with Anthropic models.
   622→
   623→**Profile tool list for Anthropic:**
   624→- `read_file` (line-numbered output, offset/limit support)
   625→- `write_file` (full file writes)
   626→- `edit_file` (old_string/new_string -- this is the native format)
   627→- `shell` (bash execution, 120s default timeout per Claude Code convention)
   628→- `grep` (ripgrep-backed with output modes: content, files_with_matches, count)
   629→- `glob` (file pattern matching sorted by mtime)
   630→- Subagent tools (maps to Claude Code's Task tool pattern, Section 7)
   631→
   632→**System prompt:** Should mirror the Claude Code system prompt structure. Cover identity, tool selection guidance, the edit_file format (explain that `old_string` must be unique), file operation preferences (edit existing files over creating new ones), and coding best practices.
   633→
   634→**Provider options:** The Anthropic profile should pass beta headers (e.g., for extended thinking, 1M context) via `provider_options.anthropic.beta_headers`.
   635→
   636→### 3.6 Gemini Profile (gemini-cli-aligned)
   637→
   638→For Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, and other Gemini models. Mirrors the gemini-cli toolset.
   639→
   640→**Profile tool list for Gemini:**
   641→- `read_file` / `read_many_files` (batch reading support)
   642→- `write_file`
   643→- `edit_file` (search-and-replace style, matching gemini-cli conventions)
   644→- `shell` (command execution, 10s default timeout)
   645→- `grep` (ripgrep semantics)
   646→- `glob` (file pattern matching)
   647→- `list_dir` (directory listing with depth options)
   648→- `web_search` (optional -- Gemini models have native grounding capabilities)
   649→- `web_fetch` (optional -- fetch and extract content from URLs)
   650→- Subagent tools (Section 7)
   651→
   652→**System prompt:** Should mirror the gemini-cli system prompt structure. Cover identity, tool usage, GEMINI.md conventions, and coding best practices.
   653→
   654→**Provider options:** Gemini profile should configure safety settings and grounding via `provider_options.gemini`.
   655→
   656→### 3.7 Extending Profiles with Custom Tools
   657→
   658→After a provider profile is loaded, additional tools can be registered:
   659→
   660→```
   661→profile = create_openai_profile(model = "gpt-5.2-codex")
   662→
   663→-- Add a custom tool on top of the profile
   664→profile.tool_registry.register(RegisteredTool(
   665→    definition = ToolDefinition(
   666→        name = "run_tests",
   667→        description = "Run the project's test suite",
   668→        parameters = { "type": "object", "properties": { "filter": { "type": "string" } } }
   669→    ),
   670→    executor = run_tests_function
   671→))
   672→```
   673→
   674→Name collisions are resolved by latest-wins: a custom tool with the same name as a profile tool overrides it.
   675→
   676→### 3.8 Tool Registry
   677→
   678→```
   679→RECORD ToolDefinition:
   680→    name        : String            -- unique identifier
   681→    description : String            -- for the LLM
   682→    parameters  : Dict              -- JSON Schema (root must be "object")
   683→
   684→RECORD RegisteredTool:
   685→    definition  : ToolDefinition
   686→    executor    : Function          -- (arguments, execution_env) -> String
   687→
   688→RECORD ToolRegistry:
   689→    _tools      : Map<String, RegisteredTool>
   690→
   691→    register(tool)                  -- add or replace a tool
   692→    unregister(name)                -- remove a tool
   693→    get(name) -> RegisteredTool | None
   694→    definitions() -> List<ToolDefinition>
   695→    names() -> List<String>
   696→```
   697→
   698→**Tool execution pipeline:**
   699→
   700→```
   701→1. LOOKUP      -- find the RegisteredTool by name
   702→2. VALIDATE    -- parse and validate arguments against JSON Schema
   703→3. EXECUTE     -- call executor with (arguments, execution_env)
   704→4. TRUNCATE    -- apply output size limits (Section 5)
   705→5. EMIT        -- emit TOOL_CALL_END event with full output
   706→6. RETURN      -- return truncated output as ToolResult
   707→```

   710→
   711→## 4. Tool Execution Environment
   712→
   713→### 4.1 The Execution Environment Abstraction
   714→
   715→All tool operations pass through an `ExecutionEnvironment` interface. This decouples tool logic from where it runs. The default runs locally. Swap in a different implementation to run the same tools in Docker, on a Kubernetes pod, over SSH, or in WASM.
   716→
   717→```
   718→INTERFACE ExecutionEnvironment:
   719→    -- File operations
   720→    read_file(path: String, offset: Integer | None, limit: Integer | None) -> String
   721→    write_file(path: String, content: String) -> void
   722→    file_exists(path: String) -> Boolean
   723→    list_directory(path: String, depth: Integer) -> List<DirEntry>
   724→
   725→    -- Command execution
   726→    exec_command(
   727→        command     : String,
   728→        timeout_ms  : Integer,
   729→        working_dir : String | None,
   730→        env_vars    : Map<String, String> | None
   731→    ) -> ExecResult
   732→
   733→    -- Search operations
   734→    grep(pattern: String, path: String, options: GrepOptions) -> String
   735→    glob(pattern: String, path: String) -> List<String>
   736→
   737→    -- Lifecycle
   738→    initialize() -> void
   739→    cleanup() -> void
   740→
   741→    -- Metadata
   742→    working_directory() -> String
   743→    platform() -> String           -- "darwin", "linux", "windows", "wasm"
   744→    os_version() -> String
   745→
   746→RECORD ExecResult:
   747→    stdout      : String
   748→    stderr      : String
   749→    exit_code   : Integer
   750→    timed_out   : Boolean
   751→    duration_ms : Integer
   752→
   753→RECORD DirEntry:
   754→    name        : String
   755→    is_dir      : Boolean
   756→    size        : Integer | None
   757→```
   758→
   759→### 4.2 LocalExecutionEnvironment (Required Implementation)
   760→
   761→The default. Runs everything on the local machine.
   762→
   763→**File operations:** Direct filesystem access. Paths are resolved relative to `working_directory()`.
   764→
   765→**Command execution:**
   766→- Spawn in a new process group for clean killability
   767→- Use the platform's default shell (`/bin/bash -c` on Linux/macOS, `cmd.exe /c` on Windows)
   768→- Enforce timeout: on timeout, send SIGTERM to the process group, wait 2 seconds, then SIGKILL
   769→- Capture stdout and stderr separately, then combine for the result
   770→- Record wall-clock duration
   771→
   772→**Environment variable filtering:**
   773→- By default, exclude variables matching: `*_API_KEY`, `*_SECRET`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_PASSWORD`, `*_CREDENTIAL` (case-insensitive)
   774→- Always include: `PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `SHELL`, `LANG`, `TERM`, `TMPDIR`, language-specific paths (`GOPATH`, `CARGO_HOME`, `NVM_DIR`, etc.)
   775→- Customizable via an env var policy: inherit all, inherit none (start clean), or inherit core only
   776→
   777→**Search operations:** Use `ripgrep` for grep if available, fall back to language-native regex search. Use filesystem globbing for glob.
   778→
   779→### 4.3 Alternative Environments (Extension Points)
   780→
   781→These are not required implementations. They demonstrate the extensibility of the interface.
   782→
   783→**DockerExecutionEnvironment:**
   784→```
   785→-- Commands execute inside a Docker container
   786→exec_command(cmd, ...) -> docker exec <container_id> sh -c <cmd>
   787→-- File operations use volume mounts or docker cp
   788→read_file(path) -> docker cp <container_id>:<path> - | read
   789→write_file(path, content) -> pipe content | docker cp - <container_id>:<path>
   790→```
   791→
   792→**KubernetesExecutionEnvironment:**
   793→```
   794→-- Commands execute in a Kubernetes pod
   795→exec_command(cmd, ...) -> kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c <cmd>
   796→-- File operations use kubectl cp
   797→read_file(path) -> kubectl cp <pod>:<path> /dev/stdout
   798→```
   799→
   800→**WASMExecutionEnvironment:**
   801→```
   802→-- For in-browser or embedded use
   803→-- File operations use an in-memory filesystem (e.g., memfs)
   804→-- Command execution is limited or emulated via WASI
   805→```
   806→
   807→**RemoteSSHExecutionEnvironment:**
   808→```
   809→-- Commands execute over SSH
   810→exec_command(cmd, ...) -> ssh <host> <cmd>
   811→-- File operations use SCP/SFTP
   812→read_file(path) -> sftp get <host>:<path>
   813→```
   814→
   815→### 4.4 Composing Environments
   816→
   817→Execution environments can be wrapped for cross-cutting concerns:
   818→
   819→```
   820→-- Logging wrapper
   821→LoggingExecutionEnvironment(inner: ExecutionEnvironment):
   822→    exec_command(cmd, ...):
   823→        LOG("exec: " + cmd)
   824→        result = inner.exec_command(cmd, ...)
   825→        LOG("exit: " + result.exit_code + " in " + result.duration_ms + "ms")
   826→        RETURN result
   827→
   828→-- Read-only wrapper (rejects all writes)
   829→ReadOnlyExecutionEnvironment(inner: ExecutionEnvironment):
   830→    write_file(path, content):
   831→        RAISE "Write operations are disabled in read-only mode"
   832→    exec_command(cmd, ...):
   833→        -- Could analyze command for write intent, or allow all
   834→        RETURN inner.exec_command(cmd, ...)
   835→```

   838→
   839→## 5. Tool Output and Context Management
   840→
   841→### 5.1 Tool Output Truncation
   842→
   843→When tool output exceeds the configured limit, it MUST be truncated before being sent to the LLM. The full output is always available via the event stream (`TOOL_CALL_END` event).
   844→
   845→**Truncation algorithm (head/tail split):**
   846→
   847→```
   848→FUNCTION truncate_output(output: String, max_chars: Integer, mode: String) -> String:
   849→    IF LENGTH(output) <= max_chars:
   850→        RETURN output
   851→
   852→    IF mode == "head_tail":
   853→        half = max_chars / 2
   854→        removed = LENGTH(output) - max_chars
   855→        RETURN output[0..half]
   856→             + "\n\n[WARNING: Tool output was truncated. "
   857→             + removed + " characters were removed from the middle. "
   858→             + "The full output is available in the event stream. "
   859→             + "If you need to see specific parts, re-run the tool with more targeted parameters.]\n\n"
   860→             + output[-half..]
   861→
   862→    IF mode == "tail":
   863→        removed = LENGTH(output) - max_chars
   864→        RETURN "[WARNING: Tool output was truncated. First "
   865→             + removed + " characters were removed. "
   866→             + "The full output is available in the event stream.]\n\n"
   867→             + output[-max_chars..]
   868→```
   869→
   870→The truncation message explicitly tells the model that output was truncated, how much was removed, and where the full output lives. This prevents the model from making decisions based on incomplete information without knowing it is incomplete.
   871→
   872→### 5.2 Default Output Size Limits
   873→
   874→| Tool         | Default Max (chars) | Truncation Mode | Rationale                                            |
   875→|--------------|---------------------|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------|
   876→| read_file    | 50,000              | head_tail       | Keep beginning (imports/types) and end (recent code) |
   877→| shell        | 30,000              | head_tail       | Beginning has startup info, end has results          |
   878→| grep         | 20,000              | tail            | Keep the most recent/relevant matches                |
   879→| glob         | 20,000              | tail            | Most recently modified files first                   |
   880→| edit_file    | 10,000              | tail            | Confirmation output, usually short                   |
   881→| apply_patch  | 10,000              | tail            | Patch results, usually short                         |
   882→| write_file   | 1,000               | tail            | Confirmation, always short                           |
   883→| spawn_agent  | 20,000              | head_tail       | Subagent results                                     |
   884→
   885→These defaults are overridable via `SessionConfig.tool_output_limits`.
   886→
   887→### 5.3 Truncation Order (Important)
   888→
   889→Character-based truncation (Section 5.1) is the primary safeguard and MUST always run first. It handles every case including pathological ones like a 2-line CSV where each line is 10MB. Line-based truncation is a secondary readability pass that runs after character truncation.
   890→
   891→The full pipeline for every tool output:
   892→
   893→```
   894→FUNCTION truncate_tool_output(output, tool_name, config) -> String:
   895→    max_chars = config.tool_output_limits.get(tool_name, DEFAULT_TOOL_LIMITS[tool_name])
   896→
   897→    -- Step 1: Character-based truncation (always runs, handles all size concerns)
   898→    result = truncate_output(output, max_chars, DEFAULT_TRUNCATION_MODES[tool_name])
   899→
   900→    -- Step 2: Line-based truncation (secondary, for readability)
   901→    max_lines = config.tool_line_limits.get(tool_name, DEFAULT_LINE_LIMITS[tool_name])
   902→    IF max_lines IS NOT None:
   903→        result = truncate_lines(result, max_lines)
   904→
   905→    RETURN result
   906→```
   907→
   908→**Default line limits** (applied after character truncation):
   909→
   910→| Tool         | Default Max Lines | Rationale                                |
   911→|--------------|-------------------|------------------------------------------|
   912→| shell        | 256               | Command output with many short lines     |
   913→| grep         | 200               | Search results, one per line             |
   914→| glob         | 500               | File listings, one path per line         |
   915→| read_file    | None              | Character limit is sufficient            |
   916→| edit_file    | None              | Character limit is sufficient            |
   917→
   918→Line-based truncation uses the same head/tail split:
   919→
   920→```
   921→FUNCTION truncate_lines(output: String, max_lines: Integer) -> String:
   922→    lines = SPLIT(output, "\n")
   923→    IF LENGTH(lines) <= max_lines:
   924→        RETURN output
   925→
   926→    head_count = max_lines / 2
   927→    tail_count = max_lines - head_count
   928→    omitted = LENGTH(lines) - head_count - tail_count
   929→
   930→    RETURN JOIN(lines[0..head_count], "\n")
   931→         + "\n[... " + omitted + " lines omitted ...]\n"
   932→         + JOIN(lines[-tail_count..], "\n")
   933→```
   934→
   935→**Why character truncation must come first:** A file could have 2 lines that are each 10MB. Line-based truncation would see "only 2 lines" and pass it through untouched, blowing up the context window. Character truncation catches this because it operates on raw size, not line count. Always truncate by size first, then by line count.
   936→
   937→### 5.4 Default Command Timeouts
   938→
   939→Every command execution has a default timeout. The model can override the timeout per-call via the shell tool's `timeout_ms` parameter.
   940→
   941→| Setting                      | Default   | Purpose                                |
   942→|------------------------------|-----------|----------------------------------------|
   943→| default_command_timeout_ms   | 10,000    | Applied when timeout_ms is not set     |
   944→| max_command_timeout_ms       | 600,000   | Upper bound (10 minutes)               |
   945→
   946→When a timeout fires:
   947→1. Send SIGTERM to the process group
   948→2. Wait 2 seconds for graceful shutdown
   949→3. Send SIGKILL if the process is still running
   950→4. Return collected output so far plus a timeout message
   951→
   952→The timeout message sent to the LLM:
   953→```
   954→[ERROR: Command timed out after {X}ms. Partial output is shown above.
   955→You can retry with a longer timeout by setting the timeout_ms parameter.]
   956→```
   957→
   958→### 5.5 Context Window Awareness
   959→
   960→The agent should track approximate token usage using the heuristic: 1 token ~ 4 characters. Emit a warning event when usage exceeds 80% of the provider profile's `context_window_size`.
   961→
   962→This is informational only. The agent does NOT perform automatic compaction or summarization (that is out of scope for this spec). The host application can use this signal to implement its own context management strategy.
   963→
   964→```
   965→FUNCTION check_context_usage(session):
   966→    approx_tokens = total_chars_in_history(session.history) / 4
   967→    threshold = session.provider_profile.context_window_size * 0.8
   968→    IF approx_tokens > threshold:
   969→        session.emit(WARNING, message = "Context usage at ~"
   970→            + ROUND(approx_tokens / session.provider_profile.context_window_size * 100)
   971→            + "% of context window")
   972→```
   973→

   975→
   976→## 6. System Prompts and Environment Context
   977→
   978→### 6.1 Layered System Prompt Construction
   979→
   980→The system prompt is assembled from multiple layers, with later layers taking precedence:
   981→
   982→```
   983→final_system_prompt =
   984→    1. Provider-specific base instructions     (from ProviderProfile)
   985→  + 2. Environment context                     (platform, git, working dir, date, model info)
   986→  + 3. Tool descriptions                       (from the active profile's tool set)
   987→  + 4. Project-specific instructions           (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, etc.)
   988→  + 5. User instructions override              (appended last, highest priority)
   989→```
   990→
   991→### 6.2 Provider-Specific Base Instructions
   992→
   993→Each profile supplies its own base prompt tuned for the model family. The base instructions should closely mirror the system prompts of the provider's native agent:
   994→
   995→- **OpenAI profile:** Mirror codex-rs system prompt. Cover identity, tool usage (especially apply_patch conventions), coding best practices, error handling guidance.
   996→- **Anthropic profile:** Mirror Claude Code system prompt. Cover identity, tool selection guidance (read before edit, edit over write), the edit_file format (old_string must be unique), file operation preferences.
   997→- **Gemini profile:** Mirror gemini-cli system prompt. Cover identity, tool usage, GEMINI.md conventions, coding best practices.
   998→
   999→The spec does NOT prescribe full system prompt text -- those are implementation details that change frequently. It specifies what topics the prompt must cover.
  1000→
  1001→### 6.3 Environment Context Block
  1002→
  1003→Include a structured block with runtime information:
  1004→
  1005→```
  1006→<environment>
  1007→Working directory: {working_directory}
  1008→Is git repository: {true/false}
  1009→Git branch: {current_branch}
  1010→Platform: {darwin/linux/windows}
  1011→OS version: {os_version_string}
  1012→Today's date: {YYYY-MM-DD}
  1013→Model: {model_display_name}
  1014→Knowledge cutoff: {knowledge_cutoff_date}
  1015→</environment>
  1016→```
  1017→
  1018→This block is generated at session start and included in every system prompt.
  1019→
  1020→### 6.4 Git Context
  1021→
  1022→Snapshot at session start. Include:
  1023→- Current branch
  1024→- Short status (modified/untracked file count, not full diff)
  1025→- Recent commit messages (last 5-10)
  1026→
  1027→The model can always run `git status`, `git diff`, etc. via the shell tool for current state. The snapshot provides initial orientation.
  1028→
  1029→### 6.5 Project Document Discovery
  1030→
  1031→Walk from the git root (or working directory if not in a git repo) to the current working directory. Recognized instruction files:
  1032→
  1033→| File Name                  | Convention       |
  1034→|----------------------------|------------------|
  1035→| `AGENTS.md`                | Universal        |
  1036→| `CLAUDE.md`                | Anthropic-aligned|
  1037→| `GEMINI.md`                | Gemini-aligned   |
  1038→| `.codex/instructions.md`   | OpenAI-aligned   |
  1039→
  1040→**Loading rules:**
  1041→- Root-level files are loaded first
  1042→- Subdirectory files are appended (deeper = higher precedence)
  1043→- Total byte budget: 32KB. If exceeded, truncate with a marker: "[Project instructions truncated at 32KB]"
  1044→- Only load files matching the active provider profile (e.g., Anthropic profile loads AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, not GEMINI.md)
  1045→- AGENTS.md is always loaded regardless of provider
  1046→

  1048→
  1049→## 7. Subagents
  1050→
  1051→### 7.1 Concept
  1052→
  1053→A subagent is a child session spawned by the parent to handle a scoped task. The subagent runs its own agentic loop with its own conversation history but shares the parent's execution environment (same filesystem, same working directory or a subdirectory). This enables parallel work and task decomposition.
  1054→
  1055→### 7.2 Spawn Interface
  1056→
  1057→```
  1058→TOOL spawn_agent:
  1059→    description: "Spawn a subagent to handle a scoped task autonomously."
  1060→    parameters:
  1061→        task            : String (required)     -- natural language task description
  1062→        working_dir     : String (optional)     -- subdirectory to scope the agent to
  1063→        model           : String (optional)     -- model override (default: parent's model)
  1064→        max_turns       : Integer (optional)    -- turn limit (default: 0, unlimited)
  1065→    returns: Agent ID and initial status
  1066→
  1067→TOOL send_input:
  1068→    description: "Send a message to a running subagent."
  1069→    parameters:
  1070→        agent_id        : String (required)
  1071→        message         : String (required)
  1072→    returns: Acknowledgement
  1073→
  1074→TOOL wait:
  1075→    description: "Wait for a subagent to complete and return its result."
  1076→    parameters:
  1077→        agent_id        : String (required)
  1078→    returns: SubAgentResult (output text, success boolean, turns used)
  1079→
  1080→TOOL close_agent:
  1081→    description: "Terminate a subagent."
  1082→    parameters:
  1083→        agent_id        : String (required)
  1084→    returns: Final status
  1085→```
  1086→
  1087→### 7.3 SubAgent Lifecycle
  1088→
  1089→```
  1090→RECORD SubAgentHandle:
  1091→    id          : String
  1092→    session     : Session           -- independent session with own history
  1093→    status      : "running" | "completed" | "failed"
  1094→
  1095→RECORD SubAgentResult:
  1096→    output      : String            -- final text output from the subagent
  1097→    success     : Boolean
  1098→    turns_used  : Integer
  1099→```
  1100→
  1101→The subagent:
  1102→- Gets its own Session with independent conversation history
  1103→- Shares the parent's `ExecutionEnvironment` (same filesystem)
  1104→- Uses the parent's `ProviderProfile` (or an overridden model)
  1105→- Has its own turn limits (configurable, default: 0, unlimited)
  1106→- Cannot spawn sub-sub-agents (depth limiting, default max depth: 1, configurable via `max_subagent_depth`)
  1107→
  1108→### 7.4 Use Cases
  1109→
  1110→- **Parallel exploration:** Spawn multiple agents to investigate different parts of the codebase simultaneously
  1111→- **Focused refactoring:** Scope an agent to a single module with a specific task
  1112→- **Test execution:** Spawn an agent to run and fix tests while the parent continues other work
  1113→- **Alternative approaches:** Spawn agents to try different solutions and pick the best one
  1114→
  1115→---
  1116→
  1117→## 8. Out of Scope (Nice-to-Haves)
  1118→
  1119→The following features are intentionally excluded from this core spec. They are valuable extensions that can be added on top of the architecture defined here. The spec's design has natural extension points for each.
  1120→
  1121→**MCP (Model Context Protocol).** An MCP client can extend the agent with tools from external servers (GitHub, databases, Slack, etc.). The tool registry supports registering MCP-discovered tools with namespaced names (e.g., `github__create_pr`). This is a natural extension but not a core requirement for a functional coding agent.
  1122→
  1123→**Skills / Custom Commands.** Reusable prompt templates stored as markdown files with YAML frontmatter. Skills standardize common workflows (e.g., `/commit`, `/review-pr`) and can be loaded from project directories or user home. The system prompt layer has a natural insertion point for skill descriptions.
  1124→
  1125→**Sandbox / Security Policies.** OS-level sandboxing (macOS Seatbelt, Linux Landlock/Seccomp, Windows restricted tokens) constrains file and network access. The `ExecutionEnvironment` abstraction provides a natural hook -- a `SandboxedLocalExecutionEnvironment` could wrap the default environment. For stronger isolation, use `DockerExecutionEnvironment`.
  1126→
  1127→**Compaction / Context Summarization.** Automatic conversation history summarization when approaching context limits. This is a complex feature with significant tradeoffs (information loss, summarization cost, pinned turns). The context window awareness signal (Section 5.5) gives host applications the information they need to implement their own strategy.
  1128→
  1129→**Approval / Permission System.** User approval gates for sensitive operations (file writes, shell commands, destructive actions). The tool execution pipeline (Section 3.8) has a natural extension point between VALIDATE and EXECUTE where an approval step can be inserted.
  1130→
  1131→**Read-Before-Write Guardrail.** Tracking which files have been read and blocking writes to unread files. A heuristic safety net that can be implemented as a tool execution middleware wrapping the execution environment.
  1132→
  1133→---
  1134→
  1135→## 9. Definition of Done
  1136→
  1137→This section defines how to validate that an implementation of this spec is complete and correct. An implementation is done when every item is checked off.
  1138→
  1139→### 9.1 Core Loop
  1140→
  1141→- [ ] Session can be created with a ProviderProfile and ExecutionEnvironment
  1142→- [ ] `process_input()` runs the agentic loop: LLM call -> tool execution -> loop until natural completion
  1143→- [ ] Natural completion: model responds with text only (no tool calls) and the loop exits
  1144→- [ ] Round limits: `max_tool_rounds_per_input` stops the loop when reached
  1145→- [ ] Session turn limits: `max_turns` stops the loop across all inputs
  1146→- [ ] Abort signal: cancellation stops the loop, kills running processes, transitions to CLOSED
  1147→- [ ] Loop detection: consecutive identical tool call patterns trigger a warning SteeringTurn
  1148→- [ ] Multiple sequential inputs work: submit, wait for completion, submit again
  1149→
  1150→### 9.2 Provider Profiles
  1151→
  1152→- [ ] OpenAI profile provides codex-rs-aligned tools including `apply_patch` (v4a format)
  1153→- [ ] Anthropic profile provides Claude Code-aligned tools including `edit_file` (old_string/new_string)
  1154→- [ ] Gemini profile provides gemini-cli-aligned tools
  1155→- [ ] Each profile produces a provider-specific system prompt covering identity, tool usage, and coding guidance
  1156→- [ ] Custom tools can be registered on top of any profile
  1157→- [ ] Tool name collisions resolved: custom registration overrides profile defaults
  1158→
  1159→### 9.3 Tool Execution
  1160→
  1161→- [ ] Tool calls are dispatched through the ToolRegistry
  1162→- [ ] Unknown tool calls return an error result to the LLM (not an exception)
  1163→- [ ] Tool argument JSON is parsed and validated against the tool's parameter schema
  1164→- [ ] Tool execution errors are caught and returned as error results (`is_error = true`)
  1165→- [ ] Parallel tool execution works when the profile's `supports_parallel_tool_calls` is true
  1166→
  1167→### 9.4 Execution Environment
  1168→
  1169→- [ ] `LocalExecutionEnvironment` implements all file and command operations
  1170→- [ ] Command timeout default is 10 seconds
  1171→- [ ] Command timeout is overridable per-call via the shell tool's `timeout_ms` parameter
  1172→- [ ] Timed-out commands: process group receives SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 seconds
  1173→- [ ] Environment variable filtering excludes sensitive variables (`*_API_KEY`, `*_SECRET`, etc.) by default
  1174→- [ ] The `ExecutionEnvironment` interface is implementable by consumers for custom environments (Docker, K8s, WASM, SSH)
  1175→
  1176→### 9.5 Tool Output Truncation
  1177→
  1178→- [ ] Character-based truncation runs FIRST on all tool outputs (handles pathological cases like 10MB single-line CSVs)
  1179→- [ ] Line-based truncation runs SECOND where configured (shell: 256, grep: 200, glob: 500)
  1180→- [ ] Truncation inserts a visible marker: `[WARNING: Tool output was truncated. N characters removed...]`
  1181→- [ ] The full untruncated output is available via the `TOOL_CALL_END` event
  1182→- [ ] Default character limits match the table in Section 5.2 (read_file: 50k, shell: 30k, grep: 20k, etc.)
  1183→- [ ] Both character and line limits are overridable via `SessionConfig`
  1184→
  1185→### 9.6 Steering
  1186→
  1187→- [ ] `steer()` queues a message that is injected after the current tool round
  1188→- [ ] `follow_up()` queues a message that is processed after the current input completes
  1189→- [ ] Steering messages appear as SteeringTurn in the history
  1190→- [ ] SteeringTurns are converted to user-role messages for the LLM
  1191→
  1192→### 9.7 Reasoning Effort
  1193→
  1194→- [ ] `reasoning_effort` is passed through to the LLM SDK Request
  1195→- [ ] Changing `reasoning_effort` mid-session takes effect on the next LLM call
  1196→- [ ] Valid values: "low", "medium", "high", null (provider default) (certain providers might have other options like `xhigh`)
  1197→
  1198→### 9.8 System Prompts
  1199→
  1200→- [ ] System prompt includes provider-specific base instructions
  1201→- [ ] System prompt includes environment context (platform, git, working dir, date, model info)
  1202→- [ ] System prompt includes tool descriptions from the active profile
  1203→- [ ] Project documentation files (AGENTS.md + provider-specific files) are discovered and included
  1204→- [ ] User instruction overrides are appended last (highest priority)
  1205→- [ ] Only relevant project files are loaded (e.g., Anthropic profile loads CLAUDE.md, not GEMINI.md)
  1206→
  1207→### 9.9 Subagents
  1208→
  1209→- [ ] Subagents can be spawned with a scoped task via the `spawn_agent` tool
  1210→- [ ] Subagents share the parent's execution environment (same filesystem)
  1211→- [ ] Subagents maintain independent conversation history
  1212→- [ ] Depth limiting prevents recursive spawning (default max depth: 1)
  1213→- [ ] Subagent results are returned to the parent as tool results
  1214→- [ ] `send_input`, `wait`, and `close_agent` tools work correctly
  1215→
  1216→### 9.10 Event System
  1217→
  1218→- [ ] All event kinds listed in Section 2.9 are emitted at the correct times
  1219→- [ ] Events are delivered via async iterator or language-appropriate equivalent
  1220→- [ ] `TOOL_CALL_END` events carry full untruncated tool output
  1221→- [ ] Session lifecycle events (SESSION_START, SESSION_END) bracket the session
  1222→
  1223→### 9.11 Error Handling
  1224→
  1225→- [ ] Tool execution errors -> error result sent to LLM (model can recover)
  1226→- [ ] LLM API transient errors (429, 500-503) -> retry with backoff (handled by Unified LLM SDK layer)
  1227→- [ ] Authentication errors -> surface immediately, no retry, session transitions to CLOSED
  1228→- [ ] Context window overflow -> emit warning event (no automatic compaction)
  1229→- [ ] Graceful shutdown: abort signal -> cancel LLM stream -> kill running processes -> flush events -> emit SESSION_END

  1253→### 9.13 Integration Smoke Test
  1254→
  1255→End-to-end test with real API keys:
  1256→
  1257→```
  1258→FOR EACH profile IN [openai_profile, anthropic_profile, gemini_profile]:
  1259→    env = LocalExecutionEnvironment(working_dir = temp_directory())
  1260→    session = Session(profile, env)
  1261→
  1262→    -- 1. Simple file creation
  1263→    session.submit("Create a file called hello.py that prints 'Hello World'")
  1264→    ASSERT env.file_exists("hello.py")
  1265→    ASSERT env.read_file("hello.py") CONTAINS "Hello"
  1266→
  1267→    -- 2. Read and edit
  1268→    session.submit("Read hello.py and add a second print statement that says 'Goodbye'")
  1269→    content = env.read_file("hello.py")
  1270→    ASSERT content CONTAINS "Hello"
  1271→    ASSERT content CONTAINS "Goodbye"
  1272→
  1273→    -- 3. Shell execution
  1274→    session.submit("Run hello.py and show the output")
  1275→    -- Verify the agent executed the command (check event stream for shell tool call)
  1276→
  1277→    -- 4. Truncation verification
  1278→    env.write_file("big.txt", REPEAT("x", 100000))
  1279→    session.submit("Read big.txt")
  1280→    -- Verify TOOL_CALL_END event has full 100k chars
  1281→    -- Verify the ToolResult sent to LLM has truncation marker
  1282→
  1283→    -- 5. Steering
  1284→    session.submit("Create a Flask web application with multiple routes")
  1285→    session.steer("Actually, just create a single /health endpoint for now")
  1286→    -- Verify the agent adjusts its approach
  1287→
  1288→    -- 6. Subagent
  1289→    session.submit("Spawn a subagent to write tests for hello.py, then review its output")
  1290→    -- Verify subagent tool calls appear in the event stream
  1291→
  1292→    -- 7. Timeout handling
  1293→    session.submit("Run 'sleep 30' with the default timeout")
  1294→    -- Verify the command times out after 10s and the agent handles it gracefully

  1299→## Appendix A: apply_patch v4a Format Reference
  1300→
  1301→The `apply_patch` tool (used by the OpenAI profile) accepts patches in the v4a format. This format supports creating, deleting, updating, and renaming files in a single patch.
  1302→
  1303→### Grammar
  1304→
  1305→```
  1306→patch       = "*** Begin Patch\n" operations "*** End Patch\n"
  1307→operations  = (add_file | delete_file | update_file)*
  1308→
  1309→add_file    = "*** Add File: " path "\n" added_lines
  1310→delete_file = "*** Delete File: " path "\n"
  1311→update_file = "*** Update File: " path "\n" [move_line] hunks
  1312→
  1313→move_line   = "*** Move to: " new_path "\n"
  1314→added_lines = ("+" line "\n")*
  1315→hunks       = hunk+
  1316→hunk        = "@@ " [context_hint] "\n" hunk_lines
  1317→hunk_lines  = (context_line | delete_line | add_line)+
  1318→context_line = " " line "\n"           -- space prefix = unchanged line
  1319→delete_line  = "-" line "\n"           -- minus prefix = remove this line
  1320→add_line     = "+" line "\n"           -- plus prefix = add this line
  1321→eof_marker   = "*** End of File\n"     -- optional, marks end of last hunk
  1322→```
  1323→
  1324→### Operations
  1325→
  1326→**Add File:** Creates a new file. All lines are prefixed with `+`.
  1327→```
  1328→*** Begin Patch
  1329→*** Add File: src/utils/helpers.py
  1330→+def greet(name):
  1331→+    return f"Hello, {name}!"
  1332→*** End Patch
  1333→```
  1334→
  1335→**Delete File:** Removes a file entirely.
  1336→```
  1337→*** Begin Patch
  1338→*** Delete File: src/old_module.py
  1339→*** End Patch
  1340→```
  1341→
  1342→**Update File:** Modifies an existing file using context-based hunks.
  1343→```
  1344→*** Begin Patch
  1345→*** Update File: src/main.py
  1346→@@ def main():
  1347→     print("Hello")
  1348→-    return 0
  1349→+    print("World")
  1350→+    return 1
  1351→*** End Patch
  1352→```
  1353→
  1354→**Update + Rename:** Modify and rename in one operation.
  1355→```
  1356→*** Begin Patch
  1357→*** Update File: old_name.py
  1358→*** Move to: new_name.py
  1359→@@ import os
  1360→ import sys
  1361→-import old_dep
  1362→+import new_dep
  1363→*** End Patch
  1364→```
  1365→
  1366→### Hunk Matching
  1367→
  1368→The `@@` line provides a context hint (typically a function signature or recognizable line near the change). The implementation uses this hint plus the context lines (space-prefixed) to locate the correct position in the file. Convention: show 3 lines of context above and below each change.
  1369→
  1370→When exact matching fails, the implementation should attempt fuzzy matching (whitespace normalization, Unicode punctuation equivalence) before reporting an error.
  1371→
  1372→### Multi-Hunk Updates
  1373→
  1374→A single Update File block can contain multiple `@@` hunks:
  1375→
  1376→```
  1377→*** Begin Patch
  1378→*** Update File: src/config.py
  1379→@@ DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30
  1380→-DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30
  1381→+DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 60
  1382→@@ def load_config():
  1383→     config = {}
  1384→-    config["debug"] = False
  1385→+    config["debug"] = True
  1386→*** End Patch
  1387→```
  1388→

  1390→
  1391→## Appendix B: Error Handling
  1392→
  1393→### Tool-Level Errors
  1394→
  1395→Tool execution errors are caught by the agent and sent to the LLM as error results (`is_error = true`). This gives the model the opportunity to recover, retry, or try a different approach.
  1396→
  1397→| Error Type          | Example                                      | Recovery                         |
  1398→|---------------------|----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
  1399→| FileNotFound        | read_file on nonexistent path                | Model can search for correct path|
  1400→| EditConflict        | old_string not found or not unique           | Model can read file and retry    |
  1401→| ShellExitError      | Command returned nonzero exit code           | Model can inspect output and fix |
  1402→| ShellTimeout        | Command exceeded timeout_ms                  | Model can retry with longer timeout |
  1403→| PermissionDenied    | Write to protected path                      | Model can choose different path  |
  1404→| ValidationError     | Invalid JSON arguments for tool              | Model can fix the arguments      |
  1405→| UnknownTool         | Model called a tool not in the registry      | Error result tells model the tool name is wrong |
  1406→
  1407→### Session-Level Errors
  1408→
  1409→These errors affect the session itself, not individual tool calls.
  1410→
  1411→| Error Type              | Retryable | Behavior                                        |
  1412→|-------------------------|-----------|--------------------------------------------------|
  1413→| ProviderError (429)     | Yes       | Retry with backoff (handled by Unified LLM SDK) |
  1414→| ProviderError (500-503) | Yes       | Retry with backoff (handled by Unified LLM SDK) |
  1415→| AuthenticationError     | No        | Surface immediately, session -> CLOSED           |
  1416→| ContextLengthError      | No        | Emit warning, session -> CLOSED                  |
  1417→| NetworkError            | Yes       | Retry with backoff (handled by Unified LLM SDK) |
  1418→| TurnLimitExceeded       | No        | Emit TURN_LIMIT event, session -> IDLE           |
  1419→
  1420→### Graceful Shutdown Sequence
  1421→
  1422→When an abort signal fires or an unrecoverable error occurs:
  1423→
  1424→```
  1425→1. Cancel any in-flight LLM stream
  1426→2. Send SIGTERM to all running command process groups
  1427→3. Wait 2 seconds
  1428→4. Send SIGKILL to any remaining processes
  1429→5. Flush pending events
  1430→6. Emit SESSION_END event with final state
  1431→7. Clean up subagents (close_agent on all active subagents)
  1432→8. Transition session to CLOSED
  1433→```
  1434→
  1435→---
  1436→
  1437→## Appendix C: Design Decision Rationale
  1438→
  1439→**Why provider-aligned toolsets instead of a universal tool set?** Models may be trained on specific tool formats. GPT-5.2-codex is trained on apply_patch; forcing it to use old_string/new_string editing produces worse results. Claude is trained on old_string/new_string; forcing it to use apply_patch produces worse results. The initial base for each provider profile should be the exact system prompt and tool harness from that provider's reference agent -- not a similar prompt, not similar tools, but a 1:1 byte-for-byte copy of the original prompt and tool definitions as the starting point. Then extend from there. Starting from the native toolset gives the best baseline experience because the model has been evaluated and optimized against exactly that harness.
  1440→
  1441→**Why an extensible execution environment instead of a fixed local implementation?** A coding agent that can only run on the local machine is limited. By abstracting tool execution behind an interface, the same agent logic works in Docker (for sandboxing), in Kubernetes (for cloud execution), over SSH (for remote development), or in WASM (for browser-based agents). The abstraction costs almost nothing in complexity but opens up major deployment flexibility.
  1442→
  1443→**Why head/tail truncation instead of just truncating from the end?** The beginning of a file (imports, type definitions, module docstring) or the beginning of command output (startup messages, headers) is often as important as the end (final results). Head/tail split keeps both. The explicit truncation marker tells the model exactly what happened so it can request specific parts if needed.
  1444→
  1445→**Why not automatic compaction?** Compaction (summarizing conversation history to free context space) is complex, lossy, and implementation-specific. Different host applications have different requirements -- a CLI might want aggressive compaction, an IDE might want to restart the session, a batch system might want to fail. The spec provides context window awareness signals and leaves the strategy to the host application.
  1446→
  1447→**Why does the loop use Client.complete() instead of the SDK's generate()?** The SDK's `generate()` function has its own tool execution loop, but it does not handle: output truncation with explicit markers, steering message injection between tool rounds, event emission for UI rendering, per-tool timeout enforcement, loop detection, or execution environment abstraction. The agent loop needs all of these, so it manages its own loop using the lower-level `Client.complete()`.
  1448→
  1449→**Why 10-second default command timeout?** This matches codex-rs. Most developer commands (compile, lint, test a single file, git operations) complete in under 10 seconds. Long-running commands (full test suites, builds) should be explicitly requested with a longer timeout. The default protects against runaway processes without being so short that normal operations fail.
  1450→
  1451→**Why exclude sensitive environment variables by default?** API keys, secrets, and tokens in the environment should not be visible to the LLM (which might include them in responses or log them). The default excludes `*_API_KEY`, `*_SECRET`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_PASSWORD` patterns. This is a safety default, not a security boundary -- the agent can still run commands that access these variables through the shell's own environment if needed.
  1452→
